steps.title: When to Call 911
steps.content:
CALL 911 IMMEDIATELY WHEN YOU SEE:
- Chest pain or pressure lasting more than a few minutes.
- Sudden severe shortness of breath.
- Uncontrolled bleeding.
- Severe burns or allergic reaction (swelling, hives, trouble breathing).
- Signs of stroke: face drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulty.
- Signs of heart attack: chest pain, sweating, nausea, pain in arm or jaw.
- A fall with suspected head injury, broken bone, or inability to move safely.
- A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes or repeating without recovery.

WHILE WAITING FOR 911:
- Stay calm and reassure the client.
- Keep the person in a safe position.
- Do not give food or drink if choking, vomiting, or unconscious.
- Control bleeding with direct pressure using a clean cloth.
- Do not move an injured person unless immediate danger is present.

AFTER CALLING 911:
Call the office as soon as you can. Document the event, time, actions taken, and emergency responders.

steps.title: Choking & CPR Awareness
steps.content:
CHOKING
A person who cannot cough, speak, or breathe may be choking. Ask, 'Are you choking?' If they nod, call 911 and follow your training. For a responsive adult, abdominal thrusts may be used if you are trained.

CPR AND AED
CPR and AED procedures may only be performed consistent with your current training and certification. If you are not certified, focus on calling 911, keeping the airway open, and providing comfort until help arrives.

HANDS-ONLY CPR
If trained, hands-only CPR means pushing hard and fast in the center of the chest at 100 to 120 beats per minute. Do not stop until help takes over or the person responds.

RECOGNIZING CARDIAC ARREST
Signs include sudden collapse, no response, no normal breathing, and no pulse. Call 911 immediately, send someone for an AED if available, and begin CPR if trained.

STAY WITHIN YOUR SCOPE
Never perform a skill you are not trained and authorized to perform. Your role is to recognize the emergency, call for help, keep the client safe, and document.

steps.title: Interactive: 911 & Medical Emergency Guide
steps.content:
MAKING THE CALL
When you call 911, stay calm. Give the address clearly, describe the problem, and answer the dispatcher's questions. Do not hang up until told to do so.

INFORMATION TO PROVIDE
- Your exact location, including apartment number or gate code.
- The client's condition and what happened.
- Any known medical conditions or medications.
- Whether the client is conscious and breathing.

GATHERING INFORMATION
Have the client's emergency contact list, medication list, and advance directives available if possible.

STAYING SAFE
If the scene is unsafe, do not enter. Wait for emergency responders in a safe location and guide them when they arrive.

NOTIFYING THE OFFICE
After calling 911, notify your supervisor or the on-call line as soon as it is safe to do so. Follow the care plan for emergency contacts.
